summary: The English of 1:1-1:6 is faithful and keeps the sayings brief, and it agrees with Bartenura and Rambam throughout; no normative comment is contradicted. The main faults are in the word data: many senses point to the wrong homograph (BDB proper names or verbs for אִישׁ, עֶבֶד, בַּיִת, אָדָם, עֶצֶם, קָנָה, דָּן, שָׁתָה, the BDB 'custom' entry for תּוֹרָה) and are moved to the Jastrow entries the pack lists, or removed where no entry fits (פְּרָס, חֹמֶר, צְרֵדָה). The model morphology has wrong construct/absolute states (כְּנֶסֶת, גְּמִילוּת, מוֹרָא, עֲפַר), wrong roots (מתן, אנש) and a wrong gender and number for רַגְלֵיהֶם, and several learner notes and two Bartenura summaries are corrected. Open questions: the variant readings in Rabbeinu Yonah's and Rambam's lemmas, which the apparatus omits, and the name 'Yehoshua' for the sage of 1:6.

value: The chain of tradition has one verb, מָסַר 'hand over', and drops it after the first link: 'Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets'.
מְסָרוּהָ (3rd plural with the 3rd feminine singular suffix, 'handed it') states the verb again in the last link, as it was stated for Moses: the chain opens and closes with מָסַר.

הֵם אָמְרוּ שְׁלשָׁה דְבָרִים introduces three plural imperatives: הֱווּ (Qal of הָיָה, Mishnaic form), הַעֲמִידוּ (Hifil of the I-guttural root עמד, 'cause to stand') and עֲשׂוּ (Qal of the III-ה root עשה).
קִבֵּל is Piel of קבל, 'received', and in Mishnaic Hebrew is the standard verb for receiving a tradition.
The third saying is a metaphor: סְיָג is a hedge round a field or a vineyard.
patches.reason: Two notes were not true: the verb does not return 'because the subject is plural' (the plural link 'the elders to the prophets' has no verb), and עמד is not a weak root.

value: Pairs (זוּגוֹת): from Yose ben Yoezer on, teachers are named two by two, so קִבְּלוּ is plural; Bartenura says the first of each pair was the nasi and the second av beit din.
בֵּית וַעַד is 'a house of meeting' for the sages; בֵּית is construct and וַעַד an absolute noun.
מִתְאַבֵּק is a Hithpael participle ('covering oneself in dust'); with וֶהֱוֵי it makes a continuing action: 'be (continually) covered'.
וֶהֱוֵי: the conjunction וְ before a ḥatef vowel takes the matching full vowel, so וֶ before הֱ; the saying has three parallel commands (יְהִי, וֶהֱוֵי, וֶהֱוֵי).
אֶת marks the definite object דִּבְרֵיהֶם, as in Biblical Hebrew; the word order puts בְצָמָא first, before the object.
patches.reason: The vowel rule was misstated ('takes ֶ before a guttural, e instead of u'): וְ takes the full vowel of the following ḥatef. אֶת before a definite object is not a Mishnaic peculiarity.

value: The mishnah has a saying of Yose (three imperatives) and then a comment in the voice of the sages ('they said', 'from here the sages said'). Bartenura notes that the comment is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's, who edited the mishnayot.
קַל וָחֹמֶר is the argument a fortiori ('light and heavy'), here without a verb: 'how much more so'.
עַל / בְּ: בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ אָמְרוּ uses ב to mean 'concerning'; the verb is plural with no stated subject ('they said' = 'people said / the sages said').
אָדָם is 'a person', but the context is a man speaking with a woman; the English says 'a man'.
גּוֹרֵם, בּוֹטֵל and יוֹרֵשׁ are participles that state a general result: 'is causing, is neglecting, is inheriting'.
שִׂיחָה is the direct object of תַּרְבֶּה / מַרְבֶּה (Hifil of רבה, 'make much'): 'make much talk', i.e. talk too much; it is indefinite, so it has no אֶת.
patches.reason: There is no infinitive in the phrase: שִׂיחָה is a noun, the indefinite object of the Hifil verb.

patches.value: Bartenura: the elders are those who outlived Joshua (Josh 24:31, שֶׁהֶאֱרִיכוּ יָמִים אַחֲרֵי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ), and these elders passed it to other elders until the first of the prophets, Eli the priest and Samuel of Ramah.
patches.reason: שֶׁהֶאֱרִיכוּ יָמִים אַחֲרֵי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ means they outlived Joshua, not that they 'lived long after' him.

patches.value: Bartenura: they were one hundred and twenty elders: Zerubbabel, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, of the days of Ezra and the return from exile in the Second Temple; among them were Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi and Nehemiah son of Hachaliah. They were called 'Great' because they restored the crown to its former state: Moses said 'the great, mighty and awesome God', Jeremiah and Daniel left out 'mighty' and 'awesome', and they restored them.
patches.reason: The summary said 'and later Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi'; the Hebrew says וּמִכְּלָלָם 'among them', and the prophets were members, not successors.

Bartenura reads עוֹמֵד as 'the world was created only for the sake of these three'; the English 'the world stands on' keeps the literal verb, nearer Rambam's 'the continuing order of the world rests on', and does not adopt 'for the sake of'. The translator's own note says so. Proposed: records.

patches.value: Rambam: when you do not know whether a man is righteous or wicked and he does something that may be taken well or badly, take it well. A man known to be righteous who is seen doing what looks wrong must be judged favourably if there is any possibility, and you may not suspect him; but of a known wicked man who does what looks good, be on guard. For the unknown man and an undecided act, the way of piety is to judge for merit.
patches.reason: Rambam says of the known righteous man ראוי שתקח אותו שהוא טוב ... ואין מותר לך לחשדו: it is a duty, not that he 'may still be judged for good'. The summary also dropped Rambam's closing ruling on the unknown man.
